sources.title: This Wonder of the Ancient World shone brightly for more than a thousand years
How to save a lighthouse? Sleep in one.
Science Makes a Better Lighthouse Lens

facts.text: Lighthouses were built to guide ships safely into harbors and keep them from crashing on the coast.
The earliest lighthouse lights were basically open bonfires burning on raised platforms.
The Pharos of Alexandria in Egypt was started by Ptolemy I and finished under his son Ptolemy II, in the third century BC.
A fire burned at the top of the Pharos tower to give its light.
The tower was named after the island of Pharos, and the word pharos came to mean lighthouse in Greek.
Lighthouse fuels changed over time: first wood and coal fires, then candles, and later lamps burning sperm whale oil, lard oil made from animal fat, and kerosene.
An open flame loses nearly 97 percent of its light; a light with a reflector behind it loses 60 to 80 percent.
Reflectors used from the late 1700s worked much like a mirror set behind a flame, gathering its light into a beam.
Before the Fresnel lens, even the brightest lighthouse beams could be seen only from about 8 to 12 miles away.
Augustin Fresnel, a scientist devoted to optics, introduced his lens design in 1822; that year the first such lens went into the Cordouan lighthouse on the Gironde River in France.
Lighthouse lenses used before Fresnel were thick, very heavy and made of poor glass, so much light was lost in them.
A Fresnel lens is made of hundreds of cut glass prisms in a brass frame; the prisms bend scattered light into one strong beam.
A Fresnel lens loses at most about 20 percent of its light.
The largest (first-order) Fresnel lenses could be seen more than 20 miles out at sea.
Before Fresnel lenses, most lighthouses showed a steady light and were hard to tell apart; a turning Fresnel lens could give each light its own flash pattern.
Before electricity, keepers lit the lamp at sunset, put it out at sunrise, and climbed the tower during the night to wind the weights that ran the clockwork turning the lens.
Keepers spent long hours cleaning and polishing; polishing the lens alone could take a whole day.
Keepers got the nickname wickies because they trimmed the burning wick so it would not smoke and dirty the lens.
U.S. lighthouses began changing to electric power in 1900; progress was slow at first and became rapid in the 1920s and 1930s.
Electric lighting left keepers with fewer duties, which cut the number of lighthouse workers and eventually led to automation.
The U.S. Lighthouse Automation and Modernization Program began in the mid-1960s.
By 1990, every U.S. lighthouse except Boston Light had been automated.
GPS and other electronic aids have made lighthouses less important for sailors, who now mainly use them as a visual aid.
Many old U.S. lighthouses have been handed to preservation groups or sold; some now serve as museums or as inns where visitors can stay the night (about 40 lighthouse inns operate in the U.S.).
